4.22.片里落点: The fear is not of saying something wrong but of failing to do it. Today: in the work group chat one person replies “I'll definitely hand it in this week”; another says nothing and hands it in on Wednesday.

4.23.title: Those who err through restraint are few
4.23.yw: The Master said: Those who go wrong through restraint are few.
4.23.常见读法: Read as “frugal people make fewer mistakes”, with restraint taken as saving money.
4.23.字眼: Xian (鲜) means few. Zhu Xi cites Xie Liangzuo: “不侈然以自放之谓约” — not letting oneself loose in extravagance is called restraint; and Yin Tun: “凡事约则鲜失，非止谓俭约也” — in all things, restraint means few errors; it does not mean thrift only.
4.23.诸家: Xie Liangzuo and Yin Tun (both cited by Zhu Xi).
4.23.片里落点: Holding back words, temper and display are all restraint, not only money. Today: the person who moves house with only two boxes is the one who loses nothing.

4.24.title: The gentleman wishes to be slow in speech and quick in action
4.24.yw: The Master said: The gentleman wishes to be slow in speech and quick in action.
4.24.常见读法: Read as “the gentleman should talk little”, taking ne (讷) as poor speaking ability.
4.24.字眼: Ne (讷) means slow of speech. Zhu Xi cites Xie Liangzuo: “放言易，故欲讷；力行难，故欲敏” — loose talk is easy, so one wishes to be slow in it; vigorous action is hard, so one wishes to be quick in it.
4.24.诸家: Zhu Xi also cites Hu Yin: “自吾道一贯至此十章，疑皆曾子门人所记也” — the ten chapters from “my Way is threaded through by one” to here were perhaps all recorded by Zengzi's disciples. This is a conjecture, and Zhu Xi records it without settling it.
4.24.片里落点: Of the easy end and the hard end, rein in the easy one (speaking) and spur on the hard one (doing). It is not refusing to speak, but not talking loosely.

4.25.title: Virtue is not solitary; it is sure to have neighbours
4.25.yw: The Master said: Virtue is not solitary; it is sure to have neighbours.
4.25.常见读法: Read as a consolation: “good people are never alone”.
4.25.字眼: Zhu Xi: “邻，犹亲也。德不孤立，必以类应。故有德者，必有其类从之，如居之有邻也” — neighbour means those close to one; virtue does not stand alone but is answered by its kind; so one who has virtue will have his kind follow him, as a dwelling has neighbours.
4.25.片里落点: This is not “good deeds are rewarded”; it is like answering like. What you hold to draws people who hold to the same thing.

4.26.title: Importune a ruler and you meet disgrace; importune a friend and you grow distant
4.26.yw: Ziyou said: In serving a ruler, importunity brings disgrace; among friends, importunity brings distance.
4.26.常见读法: Read as “don't keep bothering your boss or friends”, or reading shu (数) as “to scold”.
4.26.字眼: Shuo (数) read shuò, frequent. Zhu Xi cites the Cheng brothers: “数，烦数也” — shuo means tiresome frequency; and Hu Yin: “事君谏不行，则当去；导友善不纳，则当止” — when remonstrance with a ruler is not acted on, one should leave; when guiding a friend to good is not accepted, one should stop.
4.26.诸家: Fan Zuyu: “君臣朋友，皆以义合，故其事同也” — ruler and minister, friend and friend, are all joined by rightness, so the matter is the same. These are Ziyou's words.
4.26.片里落点: Persuasion has limits. When it does not get through, stop (with a ruler, leave); urging too often only pushes people away.

5.1.title: Gongye Chang is fit to be given a wife
5.1.yw: The Master said of Gongye Chang: He is fit to be given a wife. Though he was in bonds, it was not his crime. And he gave him his own daughter as wife. The Master said of Nan Rong: When the state has the Way, he will not be cast aside; when the state lacks the Way, he will escape punishment. And he gave him his elder brother's daughter as wife.
5.1.常见读法: Confucius married his daughter to a man who had been in prison: read as “he did not mind” or “he was broad-minded”.
5.1.字眼: Qi (妻) in the falling tone: to give a daughter in marriage. “缧，黑索也。绁，挛也” — lei is a black rope, xie is a binding; “长之为人无所考，而夫子称其可妻，其必有以取之矣” — nothing is known of Chang's character, but since the Master called him fit to marry, there must have been something to recommend him; “夫有罪无罪，在我而已，岂以自外至者为荣辱哉” — guilt or innocence lies in oneself alone; how could what comes from outside be one's honour or shame? On Nan Rong: “不废，言必见用也……以其谨于言行” — not cast aside means he will surely be employed, because he was careful in word and deed.
5.1.诸家: The Cheng brothers reject the “avoiding suspicion” reading: “此以己之私心窥圣人也。凡人避嫌者，皆内不足也……嫁女必量其才而求配” — this is to peer at the sage with one's own selfish mind; all who avoid suspicion are lacking within; in marrying a daughter one must weigh a man's ability and seek a match.
5.1.片里落点: What matters is not that Confucius was tolerant, but the one judgement “was the crime his or not”: a prison imposed from outside is not his honour or shame. The Nan Rong section says that care in word and deed stands firm in good times and bad. Today: someone once wrongly disciplined and later cleared — some people avoid him, others keep handing him the important work.

5.2.title: Of Zijian the Master said: A gentleman indeed is this man
5.2.yw: The Master said of Zijian: A gentleman indeed is this man! If Lu had no gentlemen, where could he have got this from?
5.2.常见读法: Read only as one line of praise for Zijian.
5.2.字眼: Yan (焉) read yān. Zijian's surname is Fu (宓, read fú), personal name Buqi. “上斯斯此人，下斯斯此德” — the first si refers to this man, the second to this virtue; “子贱盖能尊贤取友以成其德者……因以见鲁之多贤也” — Zijian honoured the worthy and chose friends to complete his virtue; this also shows how many worthies Lu had.
5.2.诸家: Su Shi (cited by Zhu Xi): “称人之善，必本其父兄师友，厚之至也” — in praising someone's goodness, to root it in his father, brothers, teachers and friends is the height of generosity.
5.2.片里落点: A person's virtue is taken from the worthies around him, so praising him means also praising those who made him. Today: a newcomer wins an award and the first thing said on stage is to point to a teacher in the audience.

5.3.title: Zigong asked: What about me?
5.3.yw: Zigong asked: What about me, Ci? The Master said: You are a vessel. He said: What vessel? He said: A hu-lian vessel of the ancestral temple.
5.3.常见读法: Calling Zigong a “vessel” is read as a put-down, since “the gentleman is not a vessel”.
5.3.字眼: Ru (女) read rǔ, “you”; hulian (瑚琏) read hú liǎn. “器者，有用之成材” — a vessel is a finished, useful material; the hulian is “宗庙盛黍稷之器而饰以玉，器之贵重而华美者也” — a temple vessel for millet, adorned with jade, the most precious and beautiful of vessels; “子贡虽未至于不器，其亦器之贵者欤” — though Zigong had not reached “not being a vessel”, he was a precious one among vessels.
5.3.诸家: Zhu Xi gives a single reading only.
5.3.片里落点: Two layers in one line: not yet “not a vessel”, but the most precious kind of vessel; praise with direction in it. Today: the boss says “you're the most useful person on my team”, and it feels good at the time but not quite right on the way home.

5.4.title: Yong is humane but not glib
5.4.yw: Someone said: Yong is humane but not glib. The Master said: What use is glibness? Those who meet people with a ready tongue are often disliked. I do not know whether he is humane, but what use is glibness?
5.4.常见读法: Read as “poor speakers lose out, so train your eloquence”.
5.4.字眼: “佞，口才也” — ning is a talent for speech; Zhonggong was “重厚简默，而时人以佞为贤” — weighty, simple and quiet, while people of the time thought glibness a virtue; “御，当也，犹应答也。给，辩也。憎，恶也” — yu is to meet, as in replying; ji is ready argument; zeng is to dislike; “佞人所以应答人者，但以口取辩而无情实，徒多为人所憎恶尔” — the glib answer people with argument from the mouth but no real substance, and only win much dislike; “其不佞乃所以为贤，不足以为病也。再言焉用佞，所以深晓之” — his not being glib is exactly his worth, not a flaw; saying “what use is glibness” twice is to make it deeply clear.
5.4.诸家: Zhu Xi on why Confucius would not grant him humaneness: “仁道至大，非全体而不息者，不足以当之。如颜子亚圣，犹不能无违于三月之后” — the way of humaneness is very great; only one whole and unceasing can match it; even Yan Hui, second to the sage, could not avoid lapsing after three months.
5.4.片里落点: The root problem is “no real substance”: a quick, argumentative tongue with nothing true in it wins more dislike the more it talks. Confucius did not grant Zhonggong humaneness because humaneness is too great to grant lightly. Today: the person who takes on everything, agrees to everything and delivers nothing finds colleagues walking around him three months later.

5.5.title: The Master wished Qidiao Kai to take office
5.5.yw: The Master wished Qidiao Kai to take office. He replied: I am not yet able to be sure of this. The Master was pleased.
5.5.常见读法: Declining office read as modesty or lack of nerve.
5.5.字眼: Yue (说) read yuè, pleased. “斯，指此理而言。信，谓真知其如此，而无毫发之疑也” — si refers to this principle; to be sure is to know truly that it is so, without a hair of doubt; “开自言未能如此，未可以治人，故夫子说其笃志” — Kai said he could not yet do so and was not fit to govern others, so the Master was pleased at the firmness of his aim.
5.5.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “漆雕开已见大意，故夫子说之” — Qidiao Kai had seen the main idea, so the Master was pleased. Xie Liangzuo: “至于心术之微，则一毫不自得，不害其为未信。此圣人所不能知，而开自知之。其材可以仕，而其器不安于小成” — in the subtle workings of the mind, a hair not truly gained is enough to make him not yet sure; this the sage could not know, but Kai knew it himself; his talent was fit for office, but his capacity would not rest in small achievement.
5.5.片里落点: Whether one's ability is enough, a teacher can see; the hair-thin part not truly gained inside, only oneself knows. Admitting that hair is refusing to rest in small achievement, so Confucius was glad. Today: offered a promotion, she says she can't carry that role yet and asks for another six months.

5.6.title: If the Way does not prevail, I will take a raft out to sea
5.6.yw: The Master said: If the Way does not prevail, I will board a raft and float out to sea. The one who would follow me would be You, perhaps? Zilu heard this and was glad. The Master said: You loves courage more than I do, but has nothing by which to measure things.
5.6.常见读法: Read as Confucius really wanting to retire overseas; or wu suo qu cai (无所取材) as “nowhere to get timber”.
5.6.字眼: “桴，筏也” — fu is a raft; hao (好) in the falling tone; “材，与裁同，古字借用” — cai is the same as cai “to measure”, an ancient borrowed character; “子路勇于义，故谓其能从己，皆假设之言耳。子路以为实然……讥其不能裁度事理，以适于义也” — Zilu was brave for rightness, so he was said to be able to follow; these were all hypothetical words. Zilu took them literally, and was chided for being unable to weigh the matter to fit rightness.
5.6.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “浮海之叹，伤天下之无贤君也” — the sigh about floating out to sea is grief that the world has no worthy ruler.
5.6.片里落点: Going out to sea is a sigh, a figure of speech; Zilu took it literally, with courage to spare but no sense of measuring what is fitting. Today: someone in the group chat says offhand they'll quit and travel the world, and someone else packs a bag that very night.

5.7.title: Meng Wubo asked whether Zilu was humane
5.7.yw: Meng Wubo asked: Is Zilu humane? The Master said: I do not know. He asked again. The Master said: You could be put in charge of the levies of a state of a thousand chariots; I do not know whether he is humane. What about Qiu? The Master said: Qiu could be made steward of a town of a thousand households or a house of a hundred chariots; I do not know whether he is humane. What about Chi? The Master said: Chi, with his sash tied, standing at court, could be made to speak with guests; I do not know whether he is humane.
5.7.常见读法: Confucius refusing to rate his students read as protectiveness or modesty.
5.7.字眼: Sheng (乘) read shèng; “赋，兵也。古者以田赋出兵，故谓兵为赋” — fu means troops; in antiquity troops were levied by land tax, so troops were called fu; “宰，邑长家臣之通号” — zai is the general title of a town head or household steward; chao (朝) read cháo; “子路之于仁，盖日月至焉者，或在或亡，不能必其有无，故以不知告之” — Zilu reached humaneness for a day or a month, sometimes present, sometimes absent, and it could not be guaranteed, so Confucius answered “I do not know”; “言子路之才，可见者如此，仁则不能知也” — he spoke of what Zilu's ability visibly was; humaneness could not be known.
5.7.诸家: Zhu Xi gives a single reading only.
5.7.片里落点: Say plainly what visible ability there is; humaneness comes and goes, and one does not vouch for it. Three students, three talents: each line says what they can do, none says they are humane. Today: in a background check, the referee says “I vouch for his skills; his character I can't speak to”.

5.8.title: Who is better, you or Hui?
5.8.yw: The Master said to Zigong: Who is better, you or Hui? He replied: How would I dare to look up to Hui? Hui hears one thing and knows ten; I hear one thing and know two. The Master said: You are not his equal. I grant that you are not his equal.
5.8.常见读法: Wu yu ru fu ru ye (吾与女弗如也) read as “neither you nor I is his equal”, Confucius being modest.
5.8.字眼: Ru (女) read rǔ; “愈，胜也” — yu means better; “一，数之始。十，数之终。二者，一之对也。颜子明睿所照，即始而见终；子贡推测而知，因此而识彼” — one is the beginning of numbers, ten the end, two the counterpart of one; Yan Hui's clear insight saw the end from the beginning; Zigong knew by inference, recognising that from this; “与，许也” — yu means to grant.
5.8.诸家: Zhu Xi cites Hu Yin: “子贡方人，夫子既语以不暇，又问其与回孰愈，以观其自知之如何” — Zigong liked comparing people; the Master had told him he had no time for that, and then asked who was better, he or Hui, to see how well he knew himself; “夫子以其自知之明，而又不难于自屈，故既然之，又重许之” — because he knew himself clearly and did not find it hard to yield, the Master both agreed and emphatically granted it.
5.8.片里落点: Confucius's question tests whether Zigong sees himself clearly. He does, and does not find it hard to bow, so Confucius first says “you are not his equal” and then solemnly affirms him. Today: a coach asks two players who is stronger, and one points at the other without a second thought.

5.9.title: Zai Yu slept in the daytime
5.9.yw: Zai Yu slept in the daytime. The Master said: Rotten wood cannot be carved; a wall of dung cannot be plastered. As for Yu, what is the use of scolding him? The Master said: At first, with people, I heard their words and trusted their conduct. Now, with people, I hear their words and watch their conduct. It was Yu who made me change.
5.9.常见读法: Read as Confucius scolding a student far too harshly over a nap.
5.9.字眼: “昼寝，谓当昼而寐” — daytime sleeping means sleeping in broad day; “朽，腐也。雕，刻画也。杇，镘也” — xiu is rotten, diao is to carve, wu (杇, read wū) is to plaster; “言其志气昏惰，教无所施也” — his will and spirit were dull and idle, so teaching had nothing to work on; “与，语辞。诛，责也。言不足责，乃所以深责之” — yu is a particle; zhu means to rebuke; saying he is not worth rebuking is the deepest rebuke; xing (行) in the falling tone; “宰予能言而行不逮，故孔子自言于予之事而改此失，亦以重警之也” — Zai Yu spoke well but his conduct fell short, so Confucius said that through Yu he had corrected this fault, also to warn him severely.
5.9.诸家: Hu Yin: “子曰疑衍文，不然，则非一日之言也” — the second “the Master said” may be an interpolation; otherwise these were words of different days. Fan Zuyu: “君子之于学，惟日孜孜，毙而后已……宰予昼寝，自弃孰甚焉” — the gentleman in learning is diligent every day until death; Zai Yu sleeping in the day — what self-abandonment is greater? Hu Yin: “宰予不能以志帅气，居然而倦。是宴安之气胜，儆戒之志惰也” — Zai Yu could not lead his vital spirit with his will and grew weary; the spirit of ease won and the will to vigilance slackened; “特因此立教，以警群弟子，使谨于言而敏于行耳” — Confucius merely used this to set a teaching and warn all his disciples to be careful in word and quick in deed.
5.9.片里落点: The point is not the nap but a slackened will and words that deeds do not match. “Not worth rebuking” is the heaviest rebuke. Confucius used the occasion to set a rule: hear the words, and also watch the conduct. Today: three gym memberships in a year, and not one visit.

5.10.title: I have never seen anyone who is truly firm
5.10.yw: The Master said: I have never seen anyone who is truly firm. Someone answered: Shen Cheng. The Master said: Cheng has desires; how can he be firm?
5.10.常见读法: Taking a hard temper and refusing to yield to anyone as “firmness”.
5.10.字眼: Cheng (枨) read chéng; yan (焉) read yān; “刚，坚强不屈之意，最人所难能者” — firmness means strong and unbending, the hardest thing for people to manage; “欲，多嗜欲也。多嗜欲，则不得为刚矣” — desire means many cravings; with many cravings one cannot be firm.
5.10.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “人有欲则无刚，刚则不屈于欲” — with desires one has no firmness; the firm do not bend to desire. Xie Liangzuo: “刚与欲正相反。能胜物之谓刚，故常伸于万物之上；为物揜之谓欲，故常屈于万物之下” — firmness and desire are exact opposites; being able to overcome things is firmness, so it always stands above all things; being covered by things is desire, so it always bends beneath them; “其为人得非悻悻自好者乎？故或者疑以为刚，然不知此其所以为欲尔” — was he not a prickly, self-regarding man? So some took him for firm, not knowing that this was exactly his desire.
5.10.片里落点: Firmness holds things down; desire is being covered by things. Looking hard and loving to win may mean being led by one's own desires. Today: the person who speaks most aggressively in meetings and yields to no one cannot walk past a mall sale.

5.11.title: What I do not wish others to do to me
5.11.yw: Zigong said: What I do not wish others to do to me, I also wish not to do to others. The Master said: Ci, that is not something you have reached.
5.11.常见读法: Read as another version of “do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself”, something anyone can do.
5.11.字眼: “子贡言我所不欲人加于我之事，我亦不欲以此加之于人。此仁者之事，不待勉强，故夫子以为非子贡所及” — Zigong said that what he did not want others to do to him, he did not want to do to others; this is the work of the humane, needing no effort, so the Master judged it beyond Zigong; “愚谓无者自然而然，勿者禁止之谓，此所以为仁恕之别” — in my view, wu (无, there is none) is what happens of itself, wu (勿, do not) is prohibition; this is the difference between humaneness and reciprocity.
5.11.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “我不欲人之加诸我，吾亦欲无加诸人，仁也；施诸己而不愿，亦勿施于人，恕也。恕则子贡或能勉之，仁则非所及矣” — what I do not want done to me, I also wish there to be none of from me to others: that is humaneness; what one would not want done to oneself, do not do to others: that is reciprocity. Reciprocity Zigong might manage with effort; humaneness is beyond him.
5.11.片里落点: The difference is one character, wu “there is none” against wu “do not”: having no such impulse at all is humaneness; having it and restraining it is reciprocity. What Zigong described is the humane person's naturalness, which he has not reached. Today: someone who hates being woken by messages at night schedules every message after 10 pm to send the next morning.

5.12.title: The Master's outward cultivation can be heard
5.12.yw: Zigong said: The Master's outward cultivation we may hear about; the Master's words on human nature and the Way of Heaven we may not hear about.
5.12.常见读法: Read as Zigong complaining that Confucius never spoke of nature and the Way of Heaven, or that Confucius did not discuss metaphysics at all.
5.12.字眼: “文章，德之见乎外者，威仪文辞皆是也” — wenzhang is virtue showing outwardly: bearing and speech are both it; “性者，人所受之天理；天道者，天理自然之本体，其实一理也” — nature is the heavenly principle a person receives; the Way of Heaven is the natural substance of that principle; in truth they are one principle; “盖圣门教不躐等，子贡至是始得闻之，而叹其美也” — the sage's school did not teach out of order; only now did Zigong get to hear it, and he sighed at its beauty.
5.12.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “此子贡闻夫子之至论而叹美之言也” — these are Zigong's words of admiration on hearing the Master's highest teaching.
5.12.片里落点: Wenzhang is not written essays but virtue showing in conduct and speech. Confucius spoke little of nature and the Way of Heaven, but not never; his school taught in order, and only now did Zigong hear it for the first time. The line is admiration, not complaint. Today: an apprentice in a kitchen chops vegetables for three years before the head chef first talks to her about heat.

5.13.title: When Zilu heard something
5.13.yw: When Zilu had heard something and had not yet been able to put it into practice, he only feared hearing something more.
5.13.常见读法: Read as Zilu being afraid to learn new things, as if he disliked learning.
5.13.字眼: “前所闻者既未及行，故恐复有所闻而行之不给也” — what he had heard before was not yet carried out, so he feared hearing more and not having time to carry it out (ji 给 read jǐ: to be in time).
5.13.诸家: Fan Zuyu: “子路闻善，勇于必行，门人自以为弗及也，故著之。若子路，可谓能用其勇矣” — when Zilu heard of good he was bold to carry it out; his fellow disciples felt they could not match him, so they recorded it; one like Zilu may be said to use his courage well.
5.13.片里落点: What he feared was not learning more, but the last thing not yet done. His fellow students recorded it because they felt they fell short. Today: one course not yet practised through, so don't sign up for the next.

5.14.title: Why was Kong Wenzi called “wen”?
5.14.yw: Zigong asked: Why was Kong Wenzi called “wen”? The Master said: He was quick and loved learning, and was not ashamed to ask those below him; that is why he was called “wen”.
5.14.常见读法: Read “not ashamed to ask those below” as a general virtue of diligence, unrelated to Kong Wenzi's character.
5.14.字眼: “凡人性敏者多不好学，位高者多耻下问。故谥法有以勤学好问为文者，盖亦人所难也” — people quick by nature mostly do not love learning, and those of high rank are mostly ashamed to ask those below; so the rules for posthumous names count diligent learning and asking as “wen”, for it is hard for people; “孔子不没其善，言能如此，亦足以为文矣，非经天纬地之文也” — Confucius did not bury his good points; being able to do this is enough for “wen”, though not the “wen” that orders heaven and earth.
5.14.诸家: Zhu Xi cites a Master Su on Kong Wenzi's deeds — having Taishu Ji put away his wife, then wanting to attack him, and Confucius ordering his carriage and leaving: “其为人如此而谥曰文，此子贡之所以疑而问也” — such was the man, yet he was named “wen”; that is why Zigong doubted and asked.
5.14.片里落点: Zigong asked because Kong Wenzi's reputation was poor. Confucius answered only with this one rule for posthumous names, neither defending him wholesale nor erasing his merit; “wen” goes only this far, not as far as ordering heaven and earth. Today: a boss with a so-so reputation asks an intern in front of everyone at a meeting, “I don't get this; can you explain?”

5.15.title: Zichan had four ways of the gentleman
5.15.yw: The Master said of Zichan: He had four ways of the gentleman. In conducting himself he was respectful; in serving his superiors he was reverent; in nourishing the people he was kind; in employing the people he was just.
5.15.常见读法: Read as Confucius praising Zichan point by point, showing Zichan was perfect.
5.15.字眼: “恭，谦逊也。敬，谨恪也。惠，爱利也” — gong is modesty, jing is carefulness, hui is loving benefit; “使民义，如都鄙有章，上下有服，田有封洫，庐井有伍之类” — employing the people justly means such things as capital and outlying districts having their rules, upper and lower having their garments, fields having boundaries and ditches, and households being grouped in fives.
5.15.诸家: Wu Yu: “数其事而责之者，其所善者多也……数其事而称之者，犹有所未至也……今或以一言盖一人，一事盖一时，皆非也” — when one lists someone's deeds to blame him, his good points are many; when one lists his deeds to praise him, there is still something he has not reached; now to sum up a person in one phrase, or an age in one event, is always wrong.
5.15.片里落点: Praising point by point actually shows there is still somewhere he has not reached. Respectful to himself, reverent to superiors, kind to the people, just in employing them: each of the four has its own object. Judging a person by one phrase or one event is wrong. Today: don't judge a small shop open for thirty years by one bad review.

5.16.title: Is it more polite not to stand on ceremony with old friends?
5.16.yw: The Master said: Yan Pingzhong was good at associating with others; long acquainted, he still treated them with respect.
5.16.常见读法: Once you have known someone a long time you no longer need formalities; being polite only keeps them at a distance.
5.16.字眼: “久而敬之” — long acquainted, still respectful.
5.16.诸家: Zhu Xi: “晏平仲，齐大夫，名婴” — Yan Pingzhong, a grandee of Qi, personal name Ying. He cites Master Cheng: “人交久则敬衰，久而能敬，所以为善” — when people have known each other long, respect fades; to keep respect after a long time is what makes him good at it.
5.16.片里落点: Respect fading with time is the usual course; keeping it is what “good at associating with others” means. Today: after five years sharing a flat, a roommate still knocks before borrowing your charger.

5.17.title: Was Zang Wenzhong really clever?
5.17.yw: The Master said: Zang Wenzhong housed a great tortoise, with hills carved on the capitals and water-weeds painted on the king-posts. How can he be called wise?
5.17.常见读法: Zang Wenzhong was learned and widely informed, and everyone at the time thought him clever.
5.17.字眼: “居，犹藏也。蔡，大龟也” — “ju” means to store; “Cai” is a great tortoise; “节，柱头斗栱” — “jie” are the bracket sets on the column heads; “梲，梁上短柱” — “zhuo” are the short posts on the beams; “知” is read as “zhi”, wisdom.
5.17.诸家: Zhu Xi: “不务民义，而谄渎鬼神如此，安得为知” — not attending to what is right for the people, but flattering and profaning spirits like this — how could he be wise?; “春秋传所谓作虚器，即此事也” — what the Zuo Commentary calls “making empty vessels” is this very affair. He cites Zhang Zai: “山节藻梲为藏龟之室，祀爰居之义，同归于不知宜矣” — the carved chamber for the tortoise and the sacrifice to the yuanju bird come to the same thing: not knowing what is fitting.
5.17.片里落点: Not putting his mind to what the people needed, and courting spirits instead, does not count as wisdom. Today: business is slow, and instead of asking customers, the owner spends a fortune turning the shop door to face another way.

5.18.title: Not even this counts as ren?
5.18.yw: Zizhang asked: Prime Minister Ziwen took office as prime minister three times without a look of joy, and was dismissed three times without a look of resentment. He always told the new prime minister about the affairs of the old. What do you think of him? The Master said: He was loyal. — Was he ren? — I do not know; how could he be ren? — When Cuizi killed the lord of Qi, Chen Wenzi had ten teams of horses; he gave them up and left. On reaching another state he said: “They are like our grandee Cuizi,” and left. On reaching another state he again said: “They are like our grandee Cuizi,” and left. What do you think of him? The Master said: He was pure. — Was he ren? — I do not know; how could he be ren?
5.18.常见读法: Taking office three times without joy, dismissed three times without resentment, and abandoning his fortune to leave a disordered state — how could that not be ren?
5.18.字眼: “三已之” — “yi” means to be dismissed; “十乘，四十匹” — ten teams are forty horses; “违，去也” — “wei” means to leave; in “未知，焉得仁” the “知” keeps its ordinary reading, to know.
5.18.诸家: Zhu Xi: of Ziwen, “但许其忠，而未许其仁” — he granted only his loyalty, not his ren; of Wenzi, “特许其清，而不许其仁” — he granted only his purity, not his ren. He cites his teacher: “当理而无私心，则仁矣” — to accord with principle with no selfish mind, that is ren; “子张未识仁体，而悦于苟难，遂以小者信其大者” — Zizhang did not yet know the substance of ren and was taken with hard feats, so he trusted the small to vouch for the great; “以他书考之” — checking other books, Ziwen “所谋者无非僭王猾夏之事” — all he planned was usurping the royal title and troubling the central states, and Wenzi “不数岁而复反于齐” — within a few years went back to Qi.
5.18.片里落点: Loyalty and purity are single virtues; ren asks whether one fully accords with principle and truly has no selfish mind. Trusting small things to vouch for great ones was Zizhang's fault. Today: leaving a job with a clean handover, even the password book left behind, is loyalty to duty — no more than that yet.

5.19.title: Why is thinking twice enough?
5.19.yw: Ji Wenzi thought three times before he acted. When the Master heard of it, he said: Twice is enough.
5.19.常见读法: “Think three times before you act” is usually praised as a virtue, so why did Confucius say twice was enough?
5.19.字眼: “三” here is read sàn, meaning “again and again”; “斯，语辞” — “si” is a particle.
5.19.诸家: Zhu Xi: Ji Wenzi “每事必三思而后行，若使晋而求遭丧之礼以行” — thought three times before every act, as when, sent to Jin, he first sought out the rites for a death in mourning. He cites Master Cheng: “再则已审，三则私意起而反惑矣” — by the second time it is already clear; by the third, selfish thoughts arise and confuse instead. Zhu Xi adds that when Duke Xuan usurped the throne, Wenzi “不能讨，反为之使齐而纳赂焉” — could not punish him and instead went to Qi on his behalf with bribes: “君子务穷理而贵果断，不徒多思之为尚” — the gentleman works to understand fully and values decisiveness, not mere quantity of thought.
5.19.片里落点: By the second pass things are clear; at the third, private calculation creeps in. Ji Wenzi serving a usurper as envoy is the proof of thinking oneself into confusion. Today: reading a contract for the fourth time and starting to find faults that are not faults.

5.20.title: Why is this “foolishness” harder to learn than cleverness?
5.20.yw: The Master said: When the state had the Way, Ning Wuzi was wise; when it lacked the Way, he was foolish. His wisdom can be matched; his foolishness cannot.
5.20.常见读法: “His foolishness cannot be matched” is used today as an insult — so why is this kind of foolishness harder to learn than cleverness?
5.20.字眼: “知” is read as “zhi”, wisdom; “甯” is read nìng.
5.20.诸家: Zhu Xi: Ning Wuzi “仕卫，当文公、成公之时” — served Wei under Dukes Wen and Cheng; under Duke Wen, who had the Way, “无事可见，此其知之可及也” — there was nothing remarkable to see, so his wisdom could be matched; under Duke Cheng, who lacked the Way and lost the state, he “周旋其间，尽心竭力，不避艰险……而能卒保其身以济其君，此其愚之不可及也” — moved through it all, giving his whole heart and strength, not avoiding danger, and in the end kept himself safe and rescued his lord; that is the foolishness that cannot be matched. He cites Master Cheng: “邦无道能沉晦以免患……亦有不当愚者，比干是也” — when the state lacks the Way one may keep a low profile to avoid harm, yet there are some who should not play the fool, such as Bi Gan.
5.20.片里落点: The “foolishness” is taking on what every clever person avoids, while still keeping himself safe and saving his lord; Master Cheng's mention of Bi Gan shows it is not simply feigning stupidity. Today: the year the company hit trouble everyone left, and she stayed to sort out the bad books.

5.21.title: After so many years of travel, what did Confucius go home to do?
5.21.yw: When the Master was in Chen he said: Let us go home! Let us go home! The young men of my village are ambitious and careless; they have produced something of real pattern, but do not know how to cut it to shape.
5.21.常见读法: After so many years travelling the states, what did Confucius go home to do?
5.21.字眼: “与” is read yú, a particle; “斐” is read fěi; “裁，割正也” — “cai” means to cut straight; “狂简，志大而略于事” — “ambitious and careless” means great aims but little attention to practical affairs.
5.21.诸家: Zhu Xi: “此孔子周流四方，道不行而思归之叹也” — this is Confucius' sigh of longing for home after wandering everywhere without his Way being put into practice; “夫子初心，欲行其道于天下，至是而知其终不用也。于是始欲成就后学，以传道于来世” — his original wish was to practise the Way across the world; by now he knew he would never be employed, so he began to want to form his students and pass the Way on to later ages; “不得中行之士而思其次……但恐其过中失正，而或陷于异端耳，故欲归而裁之也” — not finding men of the middle way, he thought of the next best, only fearing they would overshoot the mean and fall into heterodoxy, so he wanted to go home and shape them.
5.21.片里落点: He turns from practising the Way to transmitting it; ambitious young men can advance in the Way, but risk overshooting, so he goes home to trim them. Today: a new hire's proposal has eight good ideas in ten pages, and still needs someone to help cut it down.

5.22.title: Bo Yi and Shu Qi were so aloof — why did no one resent them?
5.22.yw: The Master said: Bo Yi and Shu Qi did not keep old wrongs in mind, and so resentment was rare.
5.22.常见读法: Bo Yi and Shu Qi were so high-minded and aloof — why did no one resent them?
5.22.字眼: “怨是用希” — “shi yong” means therefore, “xi” means few; “浼” is read měi, to soil; in “所恶” the “恶” is read wù.
5.22.诸家: Zhu Xi cites Mencius: “不立于恶人之朝，不与恶人言……望望然去之，若将浼焉。其介如此，宜若无所容矣” — they would not stand at a bad man's court nor speak with a bad man, and left in haste as if he would soil them; so fastidious, you would think no one could live with them; “然其所恶之人，能改即止，故人亦不甚怨之也” — yet once those they disliked mended their ways they stopped, so people did not much resent them. He cites Master Cheng: “不念旧恶，此清者之量” — not keeping old wrongs in mind is the magnanimity of the pure; “二子之心，非夫子孰能知之” — who but the Master could know the hearts of these two?
5.22.片里落点: So fastidious they seemed to tolerate no one, yet they stopped once a person changed, so few resented them; the measure of the pure is not keeping old accounts. Today: the neighbour you once quarrelled with apologised, and you still nod to each other on the stairs.

5.23.title: Why is borrowing something for a neighbour not upright?
5.23.yw: The Master said: Who says Weisheng Gao is upright? Someone asked him for vinegar; he begged it from his neighbour and gave it to them.
5.23.常见读法: He borrowed something on another's behalf — why would that count as not upright?
5.23.字眼: “醯” is read xī, vinegar; “乞” is read qǐ; “徇” is read xùn; in “掠美” the “掠” is read lüè.
5.23.诸家: Zhu Xi: “微生姓，高名，鲁人，素有直名者” — surname Weisheng, given name Gao, a man of Lu long reputed upright; “夫子言此，讥其曲意徇物，掠美市恩，不得为直也” — the Master says this to mock him for bending his intent to please others, taking credit and buying goodwill, which cannot be called upright. He cites Master Cheng: “微生高所枉虽小，害直为大” — the bend was small, but the harm to uprightness is great; and Fan: “是曰是，非曰非，有谓有，无谓无，曰直。圣人观人于其一介之取予，而千驷万钟从可知焉” — yes for yes, no for no, have for have, have-not for have-not: that is upright; the sage judges a man by the smallest taking and giving, and from that one knows how he would handle a thousand teams of horses.
5.23.片里落点: Saying “I don't have any” is upright; passing off a borrowed thing as your own is bending to please — a small matter, but Master Cheng says what it harms is uprightness itself. Today: a colleague asks for a charging cable, you borrow one from the next desk and say “Here, use mine.”

5.24.title: Why did Confucius find excessive politeness shameful?
5.24.yw: The Master said: Fine words, an ingratiating face, excessive deference — Zuoqiu Ming was ashamed of them, and I too am ashamed of them. Hiding resentment and befriending the man — Zuoqiu Ming was ashamed of it, and I too am ashamed of it.
5.24.常见读法: Being too polite is surely harmless — why did Confucius find it shameful?
5.24.字眼: In “足恭”, “足” is read jù; Zhu Xi: “将树反。足，过也” — pronounced jù; it means excessive; “匿” is read nì; “窬” is read yú (“穿窬”, thieves who dig through or climb over walls).
5.24.诸家: Zhu Xi cites Master Cheng: “左丘明，古之闻人也” — Zuoqiu Ming was a renowned man of old; and Xie: “二者之可耻，有甚于穿窬也。左丘明耻之，其所养可知矣。夫子自言丘亦耻之，盖窃比老彭之意。又以深戒学者，使察乎此而立心以直也” — these two are more shameful than burglary; that Zuoqiu Ming was ashamed of them shows his cultivation; the Master's “I too am ashamed” carries the sense of modestly comparing himself to Lao Peng, and deeply warns learners to examine this and set their hearts on uprightness.
5.24.片里落点: Both shames are a gap between inside and outside: sweet words, smiles and excessive courtesy to curry favour; befriending someone while nursing a grudge is pretence. Xie says it is worse than theft, because the heart is not upright. Today: holding a grudge, yet being the first at the table to raise a glass to him.

5.25.title: Why was Confucius' wish greater than Zilu's and Yan Yuan's?
5.25.yw: Yan Yuan and Ji Lu were attending. The Master said: Why not each tell me your wishes? Zilu said: I would like to share my carriage, horses, clothes and light furs with my friends, and feel no regret if they wear them out. Yan Yuan said: I would like not to boast of my good points, nor make a show of my merits. Zilu said: We would like to hear your wishes, Master. The Master said: That the old be at ease, friends have trust, and the young be cherished.
5.25.常见读法: Why is Confucius' wish greater than those of Zilu and Yan Yuan?
5.25.字眼: “盍” — why not; “衣” is read in the departing tone, to wear; “敝” — worn out; “伐” — to boast; “施” — to make a show of. Zhu Xi gives two readings of “劳”: merit (as in “劳而不伐”) or toilsome tasks (not wishing to impose them on others), and says “亦通” — either works.
5.25.诸家: Zhu Xi: “老者养之以安，朋友与之以信，少者怀之以恩” — care for the old so they are at ease, deal with friends in good faith, cherish the young with kindness; another reading, “安之，安我也；信之，信我也；怀之，怀我也。亦通” — the old are at ease with me, friends trust me, the young turn to me, also works. He cites Master Cheng: “夫子安仁，颜渊不违仁，子路求仁” — the Master rests in ren, Yan Yuan does not depart from ren, Zilu seeks ren; “子路、颜渊、孔子之志，皆与物共者也，但有小大之差尔” — all three wishes are about sharing with others, differing only in scale; and “羁靮以御马而不以制牛……须要识得圣贤气象” — bridles are for horses, not oxen... one must learn to recognise the bearing of sages and worthies.
5.25.片里落点: All three share with others, differing in scale: Zilu shares carriage and horses with friends, Yan Yuan does not boast or show off, Confucius lets each find their place, like heaven and earth nurturing without a trace. Today: the auntie in the housing block whom the elderly trust with their keys and to whose door the children run first after school.

5.26.title: Why is it so hard to see one's own faults?
5.26.yw: The Master said: It is hopeless! I have yet to see anyone who can see his own faults and bring the charge against himself inwardly.
5.26.常见读法: Why is it so hard to see one's own mistakes?
5.26.字眼: “讼” originally means to dispute (Shuowen: “讼，争也”); “内自讼” is holding a trial against oneself in one's heart; “咎” is read jiù; “鲜” is read xiǎn, few.
5.26.诸家: Zhu Xi: “已矣乎者，恐其终不得见而叹之也。内自讼者，口不言而心自咎也” — “it is hopeless” is a sigh for fear he will never see such a person; “bringing the charge inwardly” means saying nothing aloud but blaming oneself in the heart; “人有过而能自知者鲜矣，知过而能内自讼者为尤鲜。能内自讼，则其悔悟深切而能改必矣。夫子自恐终不得见而叹之，其警学者深矣” — few people with faults know them; fewer still, knowing them, can arraign themselves inwardly; one who can will repent deeply and surely change; the Master sighs for fear of never seeing it, a deep warning to learners. Zhu Xi cites no other commentator here.
5.26.片里落点: Two levels: knowing one's fault is already rare; knowing it and blaming oneself inwardly is rarer still; only self-arraignment leads to thorough change. Confucius' sigh of “never seen” is a warning to learners. Today: she misreported a figure in a meeting and nobody noticed, and after the meeting she messaged everyone to correct it.

5.27.title: The one thing Confucius claimed to have more of
5.27.yw: The Master said: In a hamlet of ten households there are surely people as loyal and trustworthy as I am, but none as fond of learning as I am.
5.27.常见读法: Is the only thing Confucius claimed to have more of than others just one thing?
5.27.字眼: “焉” is read yān; Zhu Xi: “如字，属上句” — read normally, belonging to the preceding clause (break after “如丘者焉”); the “好” of “好学” is in the departing tone; “邑” — a small settlement; “质” — native endowment.
5.27.诸家: Zhu Xi: “十室，小邑也。忠信如圣人，生质之美者也” — ten households is a small settlement; loyalty and trustworthiness like a sage's are a fine native endowment; “夫子生知而未尝不好学，故言此以勉人。言美质易得，至道难闻，学之至则可以为圣人，不学则不免为乡人而已。可不勉哉” — the Master knew by birth yet never ceased to love learning, so he said this to encourage others: fine endowments are easy to find, the highest Way is hard to hear; learning to the utmost one can become a sage, without learning one remains a villager. How can one not strive?
5.27.片里落点: Loyalty and trust are the base, found everywhere; love of learning is effort, and rare. Confucius does not boast of innate knowledge, only of loving to learn, to encourage others. The Gongye Chang book ends here. Today: honest, reliable people are everywhere; people still going to night school at sixty are few.

6.1.title: Why can one's affairs be simple but not one's heart?
6.1.yw: The Master said: Yong could be given the seat facing south. Zhonggong asked about Zisang Bozi. The Master said: He will do; he is simple. Zhonggong said: To dwell in reverence and act simply in governing the people — is that not acceptable? But to dwell in simplicity and act simply — is that not too simple? The Master said: Yong's words are right.
6.1.常见读法: Why can affairs be handled simply, but the heart must not be simple?
6.1.字眼: “南面者，人君听治之位” — facing south is the ruler's seat for hearing government; “可者，仅可而有所未尽之辞。简者，不烦之谓” — “will do” means barely acceptable, with something lacking; “simple” means not fussy; the “大” of “大简” is read tài; the “衣” of “不衣冠而处” is in the departing tone, to wear. Zisang Bozi, Hu suspects, is the Zisang Hu mentioned in Zhuangzi.
6.1.诸家: Zhu Xi: “言自处以敬，则中有主而自治严……岂不失之大简，而无法度之可守乎” — if one holds oneself in reverence, there is a master within and self-discipline is strict … otherwise is it not too simple, with no rules to keep? He cites the Kongzi Jiayu: Bozi “不衣冠而处，夫子讥其欲同人道于牛马” — lived without proper clothes and cap; the Master mocked him for wanting to make human ways like those of oxen and horses; and Master Cheng: “居敬则心中无物，故所行自简；居简则先有心于简，而多一简字矣，故曰大简” — dwelling in reverence, the heart holds nothing extra, so action is naturally simple; dwelling in simplicity, one first sets one's mind on simplicity, adding one more “simple”, hence “too simple”.
6.1.片里落点: Two kinds of “simple”: one with a master within, reverent everywhere, so affairs are naturally uncluttered; the other first intends to save effort and lets even oneself off, which becomes too simple. Confucius grants Zhonggong the south-facing seat; Zhonggong uses the question about Bozi to draw the distinction, and Confucius says “Yong's words are right.” Today: the team with the fewest rules is the one whose leader is the most punctual and orderly.

6.2.title: Why is Confucius' “love of learning” not about reading a lot?
6.2.yw: Duke Ai asked: Which of your disciples loves learning? Confucius replied: There was Yan Hui who loved learning. He did not shift his anger, and did not repeat a fault. Unfortunately his life was short and he died. Now there is none; I have not heard of anyone who loves learning.
6.2.常见读法: Why does Confucius' “love of learning” not mean reading a lot?
6.2.字眼: “好” in the departing tone; “亡，与无同” — “wang” is the same as “none”; “迁，移也。贰，复也” — “qian” is to move, “er” is to repeat; Yan Hui “三十二而卒” — died at thirty-two (as Zhu Xi records).
6.2.诸家: Master Cheng: “颜子之怒，在物不在己，故不迁。有不善未尝不知，知之未尝复行，不贰过也” — Yanzi's anger lay in the thing, not in himself, so it did not shift; whenever there was something not good he always knew it, and having known it never did it again: that is not repeating a fault; “喜怒在事，则理之当喜怒者也，不在血气则不迁” — when joy and anger lie in the matter, they are what principle calls for; not lying in the blood and breath, they do not shift; “如鉴之照物，妍媸在彼，随物应之而已” — like a mirror reflecting things, beauty and ugliness are in them; it simply responds to each. Master Zhang: “慊于己者，不使萌于再” — what dissatisfies oneself is not allowed to sprout a second time. Master Cheng on learning: “学以至乎圣人之道” — learning is to reach the Way of the sage; “约其情使合于中，正其心，养其性” — restrain the feelings to accord with the mean, rectify the heart, nourish the nature; and he ends mocking “今人乃谓圣本生知，非学可至，而所以为学者，不过记诵文辞之间，其亦异乎颜子之学矣” — people now say sagehood is innate and cannot be reached by learning, and their learning is nothing but memorising and composing — far from Yanzi's learning.
6.2.片里落点: Duke Ai asks about learning; Confucius answers with two matters of self-cultivation. Anger arises with the matter and stops when it is over, not moved on to others; a fault made once is known and not made again. Saying that since Yan Hui's death he has heard of no one who loves learning shows that love of learning lies in governing one's feelings, not in reading much. Today: scolded at work, he still crouches down at the door to tie his child's shoelaces properly.

6.3.title: Why did Confucius give one man little grain and another a lot?
6.3.yw: Zihua was sent on a mission to Qi, and Ranzi asked for grain for his mother. The Master said: Give her a fu. He asked for more. The Master said: Give her a yu. Ranzi gave her five bing of grain. The Master said: When Chi went to Qi he rode fat horses and wore light furs. I have heard that the gentleman helps the needy, not adds to the rich. When Yuan Si became his steward, he was given nine hundred measures of grain, and declined. The Master said: Don't! Give it to your neighbours and villagers.
6.3.常见读法: Both were gifts of grain — why did Confucius give one little and the other a lot?
6.3.字眼: “使、为，并去声” — “shi” and “wei” are both in the departing tone; a fu is six dou four sheng, a yu sixteen dou, a bing sixteen hu; “衣” in the departing tone, to wear; “急，穷迫也。周者，补不足。继者，续有余” — “ji” is dire need; “zhou” is making up a lack; “ji” (continue) is adding to a surplus; “毋，禁止辞” — “wu” is a word of prohibition.
6.3.诸家: Master Cheng: “圣人宽容，不欲直拒人，故与之少，所以示不当与也……求未达而自与之多，则已过矣” — the sage is tolerant and does not wish to refuse flatly, so he gave little to show it should not be given … Qiu did not understand and gave a lot on his own, which was going too far; “原思为宰，则有常禄。思辞其多，故又教以分诸邻里之贫者，盖亦莫非义也” — as steward Yuan Si had a regular salary; when he declined it as too much, the Master taught him to share it with the poor of his neighbourhood: this too was right. Master Zhang: “于斯二者，可见圣人之用财矣” — in these two cases one sees how the sage uses wealth.
6.3.片里落点: How much to give depends not on favour but on what is right. Zihua's family rode fat horses and wore light furs, not in need, so he gave only a little, refusing to add to the rich; Yuan Si's salary was owed by his post, and refusing it would be wrong, so any excess should go to his neighbours. One case is “help the needy, not the rich”; the other is “a regular salary should not be declined”.

6.4.title: Can someone of bad background be employed?
6.4.yw: The Master, speaking of Zhonggong, said: If the calf of a brindled ox is red and well-horned, even if people would rather not use it, would the spirits of the hills and rivers reject it?
6.4.常见读法: Can a person of poor background be employed?
6.4.字眼: “犁，利之反” — “li” is read lí, brindled; “骍，息营反” — “xing” is read xīng, red; “舍，上声” — “she” in the rising tone; “言人虽不用，神必不舍也” — though people may not use it, the spirits will surely not reject it.
6.4.诸家: Zhu Xi: “仲弓父贱而行恶，故夫子以此譬之……然此论仲弓云尔，非与仲弓言也” — Zhonggong's father was lowly and behaved badly, so the Master used this comparison … but this is speaking about Zhonggong, not speaking to him. Fan: “以瞽瞍为父而有舜，以鲧为父而有禹……子能改父之过，变恶以为美，则可谓孝矣” — with Gusou as father there was Shun, with Gun as father there was Yu … a son who can correct his father's faults and turn bad into good may be called filial.
6.4.片里落点: A calf of a brindled plough-ox, pure red with well-formed horns: even if people will not sacrifice it because of its origin, the spirits of hills and rivers will not reject it. A father's badness cannot cancel a son's goodness; Zhu Xi notes specifically that this speaks about Zhonggong, not to his face.
